questions.stem: Which utterance is spoken with a falling tune?

options.text: Are you coming to the assembly?
Have the scripts been marked?
Where is the assembly held?
Can I borrow your ruler?

questions.explanation: Where is the assembly held? is a wh-question, and wh-questions take a falling tune. The other three are yes/no questions, which take a rising tune. Name the sentence type first, then assign the tune.

questions.stem: The sentence 'The gate is locked.' is spoken with

options.text: a rising tune, because it ends with a full stop
a falling tune, because it is a statement
a rising tune, because it gives new information
a level tune, because it is short

questions.explanation: Statements take a falling tune. The full stop marks writing, not pitch; new information does not by itself raise the voice at the end; and English does not use a special 'level' tune for short sentences in this paper.

distractorRationale.a: The full stop is a punctuation mark; the tune is decided by the sentence type
distractorRationale.c: Giving information is exactly what a falling statement does
distractorRationale.d: Length does not choose the tune; function does

questions.stem:
In the following sentence the emphatic stress is on the capitalised word. Choose the question to which the sentence is the appropriate answer.

Adaeze bought a NEW bag.

options.text: Did Tunde buy a new bag?
Did Adaeze steal a new bag?
Did Adaeze buy an old bag?
Did Adaeze buy a new shoe?

questions.explanation: NEW is the contrasted idea, so the question must replace new with a contrasting word such as old and leave Adaeze, buy and bag unchanged. That is the WAEC emphatic-stress rule: only the capitalised word is in dispute.

distractorRationale.a: Changes the buyer; that would require ADAEZE in capitals
distractorRationale.b: Changes the verb; that would require BOUGHT in capitals
distractorRationale.d: Changes the object; that would require BAG in capitals

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Oral English

questions.stem:
Choose the question to which this sentence is the appropriate answer.

The teacher PUNISHED the boy.

options.text: Did the principal punish the boy?
Did the teacher praise the boy?
Did the teacher punish the girl?
Did the teacher punish the boys?

questions.explanation: PUNISHED is the emphatic word, so the matching question contrasts the action — praise instead of punish — and keeps teacher and boy. Changing principal, girl or boys would require a different word in capitals.

distractorRationale.a: Contrasts the doer; that would capitalise TEACHER
distractorRationale.c: Contrasts the object; that would capitalise BOY
distractorRationale.d: Contrasts number; that would still capitalise BOY, not PUNISHED

questions.stem: Which of these yes/no questions is correctly assigned a rising tune?

options.text: What is your name? ↗
Who took the chalk? ↗
Have you eaten? ↗
Close the door. ↗

questions.explanation: Have you eaten? is a yes/no question, so the rising tune is correct. What and who questions are wh-questions and should fall. Close the door is a command and should fall.

questions.stem: What meaning does the capitalisation convey in 'TUNDE stole the money yesterday'?

options.text: It was not Chinedu who stole it; it was Tunde
Tunde borrowed the money rather than stealing it
Tunde stole the phone, not the money
The theft happened last week, not yesterday

questions.explanation: Emphatic stress on TUNDE contrasts the person. The speaker insists on the identity of the thief and takes the rest of the sentence as given. Stressing stole, money or yesterday would produce the other three meanings.

distractorRationale.b: That meaning needs STOLE in capitals
distractorRationale.c: That meaning needs MONEY in capitals
distractorRationale.d: That meaning needs YESTERDAY in capitals

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Oral English

questions.stem:
Choose the question to which this sentence is the appropriate answer.

Musa travelled to Kano LAST WEEK.

options.text: Did Musa travel to Abuja last week?
Did Bola travel to Kano last week?
Did Musa travel to Kano last month?
Did Musa fly to Kano last week?

questions.explanation: LAST WEEK is the emphatic element, so the question must contrast the time — last month, yesterday, this morning — and keep Musa, travel and Kano. Changing the destination, the traveller or the means of travel would require a different capitalised word.

distractorRationale.a: Contrasts Kano; that would capitalise KANO
distractorRationale.b: Contrasts Musa; that would capitalise MUSA
distractorRationale.d: Contrasts travelled; that would capitalise TRAVELLED

sources.title: WAEC English Language Syllabus — Oral English

questions.stem: A speaker says 'Is the hall free?' with a falling tune instead of a rising one. What is the most likely effect?

options.text: It will sound like a genuine request for a yes or no
It will sound more like a challenge or a statement expecting agreement than a simple enquiry
It will turn the sentence into a wh-question
It will make the word hall carry emphatic stress automatically

questions.explanation: A yes/no question with a rising tune is an open enquiry. The same words with a fall can sound as if the speaker already knows, is checking, or is challenging. Tune does not rewrite the grammar into a wh-question, and it is not the same device as emphatic stress on one word.

distractorRationale.a: That is the effect of the rising tune this speaker failed to use
distractorRationale.c: Wh-questions are formed with who, what, where and the rest, not by changing pitch alone
distractorRationale.d: Emphatic stress is extra force on a chosen word, not a side-effect of a falling yes/no question
